title: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm
summary: Dissolution of a firm ends the business relationship among all partners; assets are realised, liabilities are paid and the balance is settled with the partners. This chapter covers the modes of dissolution, settlement of accounts under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, and preparation of the Realisation Account, partners' capital accounts and the cash or bank account.

notes.heading: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm
notes.html:
BasisDissolution of partnershipDissolution of firm
MeaningChange in the existing relationship among partners (reconstitution)Breakdown of relationship among all partners; business closes
BusinessContinuesComes to an end
Books of accountNot closedClosed
Assets and liabilitiesRevalued (Revaluation A/c)Realised and paid (Realisation A/c)
Court interventionNot involvedMay be ordered by court
EffectDissolution of partnership may or may not lead to dissolution of firmDissolution of firm always means dissolution of partnership

notes.heading: Modes of dissolution of a firm
notes.html:
1. By agreement (Section 40): with the consent of all partners or as per a contract.
  2. Compulsory dissolution (Section 41): when all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent; or when the business becomes illegal.
  3. On happening of certain contingencies (Section 42): expiry of the fixed term; completion of the venture for which the firm was formed; death of a partner; insolvency of a partner (subject to contract).
  4. By notice (Section 43): in a partnership at will, any partner may give written notice of his intention to dissolve.
  5. By court (Section 44): on a suit by a partner when a partner becomes of unsound mind or permanently incapable; is guilty of misconduct; persistently breaches the agreement; transfers his whole interest to a third party; the business can be carried on only at a loss; or any other just and equitable ground.

notes.heading: Settlement of accounts: Section 48
notes.html:
Losses (including deficiency of capital) are paid in this order: first out of profits, then out of capital, and finally by partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.

Assets of the firm (including amounts contributed by partners to make up deficiency) are applied in this order:

  1. Debts of the firm to third parties (outside liabilities)
  2. Loans and advances made by partners (as distinct from capital), proportionately
  3. Capital of each partner, proportionately
  4. The surplus, if any, among partners in profit-sharing ratio

Private debts vs firm's debts (Section 49): firm's property is used first for the firm's debts and a partner's private property first for his private debts; any surplus from either side can then be used for the other.

notes.heading: Realisation Account: what goes where
notes.html:
Debit side (Dr)Credit side (Cr)
All assets at book value (except cash, bank, fictitious assets and partners' loans to the firm)All outside liabilities at book value (creditors, bills payable, bank loan, outstanding expenses, spouse's loan)
Cash paid for liabilitiesProvisions against assets (provision for doubtful debts, accumulated depreciation, investment fluctuation reserve to the extent of investments)
Realisation expenses paid by the firm, or by a partner on its behalfCash received from sale of assets (recorded and unrecorded)
Unrecorded liabilities paidAssets taken over by partners (at agreed value)
Profit on realisation (transferred to partners in PSR)Loss on realisation (transferred to partners in PSR)

Not transferred: cash and bank (they are the medium of settlement), partners' capitals, partners' loans, accumulated profits and losses (these go directly to capital accounts in PSR).

notes.heading: Worked illustration 1: complete dissolution
notes.html:

Assets: Bank ₹15,000; Debtors ₹35,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹40,000 (total ₹1,70,000). notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Transferring a partner's loan to the Realisation Account; it is paid directly through the bank after outside liabilities.
  • Transferring cash or bank balance to the Realisation Account.
  • Passing an entry when a creditor accepts an asset in full settlement.
  • Debiting the provision for doubtful debts instead of crediting it to Realisation.
  • Distributing reserves through the Realisation Account instead of directly to capitals.
  • Recording actual expenses instead of the agreed remuneration when a partner has agreed to bear them.
  • Not checking that the bank account closes at nil after final payments.

keyTerms.definition: Ending of partnership among all partners, closure of business and settlement of accounts.
Change in the relationship among partners while the firm continues, e.g. on admission or retirement.
Nominal account prepared on dissolution to record sale of assets, payment of liabilities and the resulting profit or loss.
Dissolution required by law when all or all but one partners become insolvent or the business becomes unlawful (Section 41).
Dissolution ordered by a court on a partner's petition on grounds listed in Section 44.
Partnership with no fixed term, which any partner may dissolve by written notice (Section 43).
Asset not shown in the books (e.g. fully written-off furniture); its realisation is credited to the Realisation Account.
Liability not in the books; its payment is debited to the Realisation Account.
Costs of winding up the business, debited to the Realisation Account.
Provision laying down the order of settling losses and applying assets on dissolution.

formulas.name: Profit or loss on realisation
formulas.html: (Liabilities and provisions transferred + Assets realised + Assets taken over by partners) − (Assets transferred + Liabilities paid + Realisation expenses)

formulas.name: Final settlement with partner
formulas.html: Opening capital + Share of reserves + Realisation profit + Liabilities taken over + Expenses paid/remuneration − Realisation loss − Assets taken over − Share of accumulated losses

formulas.name: Check on bank account
formulas.html: Opening balance + Realisations − Liabilities paid − Expenses − Partners' loans − Final payments to partners = Nil

mcqs.q: On dissolution of a firm, assets are transferred to the Realisation Account at:
options: Market value
Book value
Realisable value
Replacement value
mcqs.explanation: Assets are closed at book value; the difference with the amount realised becomes profit or loss on realisation.

mcqs.q: A loan given by a partner to the firm is, on dissolution:
options: Transferred to the Realisation Account
Transferred to his capital account
Paid after outside liabilities but before capitals
Paid after capitals are returned
mcqs.explanation: Section 48 places partners' loans after outside debts but before capital.

mcqs.q: A firm must be compulsorily dissolved when:
options: The term of the firm expires
Partners mutually agree
All partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
A partner gives notice
mcqs.explanation: Section 41 makes dissolution compulsory on insolvency of all or all but one partner, or if the business becomes illegal.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Cash and bank balances are not transferred to the Realisation Account.
Reason (R): They are already in liquid form and are used to settle liabilities and partners' claims.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: There is nothing to realise in cash; it is the medium of settlement. R explains A.

mcqs.q: Creditors of ₹50,000 accepted machinery valued at ₹45,000 and the balance in cash. The entry will be:
options: No entry
Creditors A/c Dr To Machinery A/c ₹45,000
Realisation A/c Dr To Bank A/c ₹50,000
Realisation A/c Dr To Bank A/c ₹5,000
mcqs.explanation: Only the cash part of the settlement is recorded; creditors and machinery are already in the Realisation Account.

mcqs.q: Case: Assets (other than bank) of ₹1,55,000 and liabilities of ₹50,000 were transferred to the Realisation Account. Assets realised ₹98,000 in cash and a partner took over stock for ₹45,000. Liabilities were paid ₹48,000 and expenses ₹2,000. The result of realisation is:
options: Profit ₹12,000
Profit ₹2,000

mcqs.q: On dissolution, provision for doubtful debts appearing in the balance sheet is:
options: Debited to Realisation A/c
Credited to Realisation A/c
Credited to partners' capital accounts
Ignored
mcqs.explanation: Debtors are transferred at gross value, so the provision against them is credited to the Realisation Account.

mcqs.q: A partner agreed to bear all realisation expenses for a remuneration of ₹5,000. Actual expenses of ₹4,000 were paid by him. The entry is:
options: Realisation A/c Dr To Partner's Capital A/c ₹5,000
Realisation A/c Dr To Bank A/c ₹4,000
Partner's Capital A/c Dr To Bank A/c ₹4,000
Realisation A/c Dr To Partner's Capital A/c ₹4,000
mcqs.explanation: The firm's cost is only the agreed remuneration; the actual expenses are the partner's own concern.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Under Section 48, partners' loans are repaid before outside creditors.
Reason (R): Partners are the owners of the firm.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Outside creditors are paid first, so A is false; it is true that partners are owners, which is why their claims rank after outsiders.

mcqs.q: A court may order dissolution of a firm under Section 44 when:
options: The term of the firm expires
All partners agree to dissolve
A partner becomes of unsound mind
The business becomes unlawful
mcqs.explanation: Unsound mind of a partner is a ground for court dissolution; expiry of term and agreement are contingency/agreement modes; illegality causes compulsory dissolution.

mcqs.q: An unrecorded asset taken over by a partner on dissolution is recorded as:
options: Realisation A/c Dr To Partner's Capital A/c
Partner's Capital A/c Dr To Realisation A/c
Asset A/c Dr To Realisation A/c
No entry
mcqs.explanation: The partner receives an asset, so his capital is debited and the Realisation Account is credited with the agreed value.

mcqs.q: A loan given to the firm by a partner's wife is, on dissolution:
options: Transferred to the partner's capital account
Transferred to the credit of Realisation Account
Paid after partners' loans
Transferred to the debit of Realisation Account
mcqs.explanation: The wife is an outsider, so her loan is an outside liability credited to Realisation and paid along with other outside liabilities.

questions.q: State one difference between dissolution of partnership and dissolution of a firm.
questions.answerHtml: On dissolution of partnership the business continues and books are not closed, whereas on dissolution of a firm the business comes to an end and all books are closed.

questions.q: Why is a Realisation Account prepared on dissolution of a firm?
questions.answerHtml: To record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities and to find the net profit or loss on realisation, which is shared by partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

questions.q: State the order in which the assets of a firm are applied on dissolution as per Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
questions.answerHtml:
1. In paying debts of the firm to third parties.
  2. In paying each partner proportionately what is due to him for loans and advances (as distinct from capital).
  3. In paying each partner proportionately what is due on account of capital.
  4. The residue, if any, is divided among partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

Losses, including deficiency of capital, are met first from profits, then from capital and lastly by partners individually in PSR.

questions.q: Explain any four modes of dissolution of a partnership firm.
questions.answerHtml:
1. By agreement (Sec 40): with the consent of all partners or under a contract.
  2. Compulsory (Sec 41): when all or all but one partners are insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful.
  3. On contingencies (Sec 42): expiry of term, completion of venture, death or insolvency of a partner.
  4. By notice (Sec 43): in a partnership at will, by written notice of any partner.
  5. By court (Sec 44): e.g. unsound mind or misconduct of a partner, persistent breach of agreement, or business possible only at a loss.
